<section class="band">
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow">Two engines</p>

## Rules, a local AI model, *or both*

You choose the engine on each run.

::::: {.two}
::: {.card}
[No AI of any kind]{.kicker}

### The rules engine
It reads with written rules and the layout of the page. A scanned page is first turned into text by OCR (optical character recognition). The same document always gives the same output, so the code and the manual call it the deterministic engine. Every value records the rule that found it and where on the page it was found. It uses no AI and no network connection, so agencies whose policies do not permit AI tools can use it alone.
:::

::: {.card}
[Optional]{.kicker}

### The local AI engine
A language model reads the page images. It runs on your own computer through Ollama, a free program that runs AI models locally, and it sends nothing to any cloud service. It reads what rules and OCR cannot, handwriting above all.
:::
:::::

When you run both, the package compares the two addresses on every document and flags each disagreement for a person to review. Either engine also flags a value it is unsure of. Neither guesses a value to keep a row looking complete.
::::::
</section>

<section class="band-dark">
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow on-dark">Privacy</p>

## Your documents stay on *your computer* {.on-dark}

Court filings carry tenants' names and addresses. With the default engines, the documents, the page images, and the extracted values never leave your computer. The package sends no usage data, and once installed it runs with the network unplugged. Every example and test document in the code repository is made up.
::::::
</section>

<section>
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow">Accuracy</p>

## Grade a random 50 before you *trust a run*

The Eviction Research Network wrote and measured the rules on Washington State filings. Another court's forms, scan quality, or decade can make them misread a field without raising a flag, and accuracy differs by field. On a random 50 King County summonses from 2017, the rules engine read the street right on about 85 percent and the plaintiff on about 40 percent (October 2026).

So the first run is a random 50 of your own documents. You grade them on a review page that shows each document beside what the engine read. The package scores the engine against your answers. You scan the whole folder only when the fields you need are accurate enough.

### What grading is for {#grading}

Grading happens on your own computer, and it does three things for your own run.

::::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.n}

### It measures the engine
The score counts, field by field, how often the engine was right on your documents. You decide from it which fields are accurate enough to use.
:::

::: {.card}
[2]{.n}

### It corrects your table
Every document you grade carries your answer in the final table, in place of the engine's.
:::

::: {.card}
[3]{.n}

### It teaches the engine your form
The boxes you draw show where your court's form prints each field. The package learns a template from them and uses it only after you approve it.
:::
:::::

### How the rules improve {#rules}

Grading does not change the rules that read the text. A person changes them, in one of two ways. You can change them on your own copy of the package, and [Changing the rules](https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/blob/main/docs/changing_rules.md){target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"} shows how. Or the Eviction Research Network can write rule improvements from your corrections and release them in the package, where every user gets them. Corrections hold tenants' names and addresses, so that takes a data agreement between your organization and UC Berkeley before anything is sent. Write to [evictions@berkeley.edu](mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=extract-text) to ask.

[How grading and accuracy work](how-it-works.html#accuracy){.more}
::::::
</section>

<section class="band">
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow">First steps</p>

## Getting started, *in outline*

The Get started page has seven steps, each a few lines of R to copy and run. They fall into three stages.

::::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[1]{.n}

[Steps 1 and 2]{.kicker}

### Install
Install four free programs that open PDFs, read scanned pages, and run the engine (poppler, tesseract, Python, and git), then extract-text itself. A checkup looks at your computer and names anything missing.
:::

::: {.card}
[2]{.n}

[Steps 3 to 5]{.kicker}

### Test on a sample
Read a made-up summons, scan a random 50 of your own documents, grade them on the review page, and score the engine.
:::

::: {.card}
[3]{.n}

[Steps 6 and 7]{.kicker}

### Run the whole folder
Scan every document, grade a second random 50, and build the final table of cases.
:::
:::::

::: {.actions style="margin-top: 34px;"}
[Get started](get-started.html){.btn}
[Read the manual](https://github.com/evictionresearch/extract-text/blob/main/docs/manual.md){.btn .ghost target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"}
:::
::::::
</section>

<section>
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow">Uses</p>

## Who extract-text *is for*

The Eviction Research Network built extract-text for work that describes or reduces displacement. That work includes research, legal services, journalism, policy analysis, court administration, and tenant defense.

Running extract-text takes someone who works in R, Python, or a terminal. If that is not you, send this page to an analyst on your staff or at a partner organization, or write to [evictions@berkeley.edu](mailto:evictions@berkeley.edu?Subject=extract-text).

An eviction filing is not a finding of wrongdoing. The project does not support tenant screening, landlord blacklists, debt collection, or the use of these records to locate people for enforcement.

[Read the terms of use](about.html#terms){.more}
::::::
</section>

<section class="band">
:::::: {.wrap .sec}
<p class="eyebrow">Publications</p>

## The research *behind it*

::::: {.cards}
::: {.card}
[Cityscape, 2024]{.kicker}

### Toward a National Eviction Data Collection Strategy Using Natural Language Processing
Thomas, Ramiller, Ren, and Toomet describe the method this package grew from and apply it to more than 110,000 Washington eviction filings from 2004 to 2017.

[Read about the paper](about.html#research){.more}
:::

::: {.card}
[Dissertation, UC Berkeley, 2024]{.kicker}

### Not All Eviction Cases are Alike
Cheng Ren read 772,629 court files from 56,070 Pierce County cases, 2004 to 2022, and followed each case past the filing to dismissal, judgment, and the sheriff.

[Read about the dissertation](about.html#research){.more}
:::

::: {.card}
[People]{.kicker}

### Cheng Ren, Tim Thomas, and Aaron Culich
The authors work at the University at Albany, SUNY, and the University of California, Berkeley.

[Meet the authors](about.html#authors){.more}
:::
:::::
::::::
</section>

## Development *timeline* {#development}

extract-text is being built in three stages. The first is released, and the other two are open. Until all three are done, command options and output columns can still change between releases.

```{=html}
<ol class="timeline">
<li class="done">
<span class="mark" aria-hidden="true"><svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="16" height="16"><path d="M5 12.5l4.5 4.5L19 7.5" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/></svg></span>
<div>
<p class="status">Stage 1 · Done</p>
<h3>The rules engine</h3>
<p>The engine reads the parties, the address, the attorney, and the case number with written rules and no AI. It is released, along with the review page for grading and form templates. Its rules keep improving as graded documents come in.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li class="open">
<span class="mark" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<div>
<p class="status">Stage 2 · Open</p>
<h3>Local AI integration and improvements</h3>
<p>The local AI engine runs today as an option. The work that remains is to measure it against hand-graded documents, improve what it reads, and make it easier to set up.</p>
</div>
</li>
<li class="open">
<span class="mark" aria-hidden="true"></span>
<div>
<p class="status">Stage 3 · Open</p>
<h3>Large text evaluation</h3>
<p>Future versions are planned to read the body of a filing, such as the reason for the eviction.</p>
</div>
</li>
</ol>
```
